transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-02-25 15:30 UTC
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Pyralis Eng Lead), Priya Desai (Pyralis CTO), Jordan Miles (SRE), Nora Kim (Product)

Summary:
High-level POC scoping to align on traffic characterization, success criteria for latency/cost/accuracy, what telemetry/logs Pyralis can share, and an initial benchmark timeline. Focus on concurrency vs QPS, token-length distribution for prompt+response, and acceptable SLOs for tail latency.

Topics covered:
- Traffic shape and bursts (episodic vs steady)
- Typical QPS and concurrent inference patterns
- Token distribution (input prompt length vs generated tokens) and token skews across cohorts
- Benchmark KPIs: p50/p95/p99 latencies, cost per 1k tokens, correctness/regression checks
- Data/security requirements: VPC, KMS, audit logs, SOC2 questions
- Next steps and artifact handoffs (traffic template, scrubbed logs, benchmark schedule)

Action items (listed in call notes): see action_items metadata

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining on short notice, I think we have about 50 minutes, um so quick intros?
[00:00:08] Alex Rivera (Pyralis): Alex, engineering, I run infra for inference and ops, hey.
[00:00:11] Priya Desai (Pyralis CTO): Priya here, CTO, I'll be focused on success criteria and compliance side.
[00:00:15] Jordan Miles (SRE): Jordan, SRE, we'll handle the logs and replay.
[00:00:18] Nora Kim (Product): Nora, product, focusing on latency targets for the user flows.
[00:00:21] Samir Patel (Redwood SE): Samir, I'm the systems SE, I'll lead the benchmark configs and runbooks.

[00:00:30] Maya: Great. Goal for today: we want to map your traffic, agree on success metrics for the POC, and leave with a clear data handoff and schedule. We'll propose a benchmark plan you can run or we can run in your VPC depending on preference. Sound right?
[00:00:40] Priya: Yep; also want to confirm security boundaries early — VPC, KMS for keys, audit logs.

[00:00:50] Samir: Totally — we'll cover those. Alex, can you walk through your traffic shape? QPS, peaks, concurrent requests?
[00:00:58] Alex: Sure. So daily volume is modest but spiky. Baseline is about 7-10 QPS average during business hours, spikes up to 220 QPS for short bursts, usually two or three times a day for 2–5 minutes. Concurrency from our side is complicated — for chat sessions we hold long-running sessions, so you get many concurrent open KV caches but low per-second token emit during typing. For synchronous calls we see bursts where 40–60 concurrent requests hit the endpoint, but during the big spikes it can reach 140 concurrent in the busiest 30s.
[00:01:36] Maya: Okay so bursty episodic behavior with a mix of short sync calls and longer chat sessions. Jordan, can you share token length distributions?
[00:01:44] Jordan: We looked at averages: prompts cluster around 60–120 tokens, but we have a tail — some search/summary flows push 800–1200 prompt tokens. Output lengths are variable: most responses are 20–80 tokens, with a small cohort for long explanations that are 400–800 tokens. On percentiles: p50 prompt ~85 tokens, p95 ~420, p99 ~980. Response p50 ~45 tokens, p95 ~280, p99 ~720. There's also token-skew by cohort: helpdesk flows have shorter prompts and longer responses, while search flows are long prompts short responses.
[00:02:29] Samir: That token tail matters a lot for GPU memory and KV cache. For benchmarking we usually create three mixes: short (50/30), medium (200/100), long-tail (800/400) — numbers are prompt/response. Does that map to your flows?
[00:02:42] Alex: Yes, that'd work. The long-tail is about 2% of traffic but drives most memory usage.

[00:02:50] Nora: For product success, p95 end-to-end latency should be under 350ms for chat quick replies, and under 1.2s for longer completions. If p99 goes above 2.5s we get user complaints. Cost target is also important — we want to understand cost per 1k tokens and tradeoffs with latency.
[00:03:08] Priya: From an org level, we need audit logs and SSO/SAML. Also SOC 2 scope — can Redwood provide the compliance docs and a data flow diagram?
[00:03:18] Maya: Yes, we'll share the SOC2 pack and our data flow diagram. For VPC/private we can discuss a dedicated connector, and KMS integration for keys, plus audit log retention options. I'll add that to the handoff.

[00:03:30] Samir: On benchmark KPIs: we'll measure tokenized throughput, end-to-end latency (inference only and end-to-end), tail quantiles p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU utilization, memory pressure, KB cache hit rates, and cost per 1k tokens under the chosen batching strategy. We'll also do correctness/regression checks using a small eval set you provide.
[00:03:52] Jordan: On telemetry — we can export request level: timestamp, request_id, prompt_token_count, response_token_count, latency_ms, user_cohort, region. Is that enough?
[00:03:59] Samir: Perfect. For a useful replay we need a time-ordered log with those fields. Anonymize ids please. Also include headers that indicate whether the call is streaming vs non-streaming, and any function calls / tool-use flags.

[00:04:13] Alex: How intrusive is the replay? Do you spin up instances in our VPC or do you run it against Redwood hosted endpoints?
[00:04:18] Maya: We have three options: 1) you give us logs and we run the replay in our hosted test environment using synthetic data; 2) we provide a replay harness you run inside your VPC with Redwood agents; 3) run the benchmark live against a dedicated Redwood Dedicated pool if you have a dedicated contract. For an initial POC most customers prefer option 2 (local replay) or option 1 if sharing logs is easier.
[00:04:36] Priya: We prefer the replay in our VPC for data residency reasons, but we want Redwood to provide a runbook and the harness.

[00:04:44] Samir: We can provide a Dockerized replay harness and a small infra template (Terraform) to run inside your VPC. We'll also provide a config with concurrency shaping, QPS throttles, and a token-length mix generator.
[00:04:56] Alex: Good. For KPIs, we need to validate: sustained throughput at target QPS, cold-start tail behaviour, and graceful degradation when GPUs saturate.
[00:05:04] Samir: Right — we'll instrument graceful fallbacks to smaller quantized model variants and measure quality delta. We'll include automatic fallbacks in the playbook.

[00:05:12] Nora: Can we have an estimate of hardware footprint for your suggested configs? Like how many GPUs for steady 50 QPS with our token mix vs peak 220 QPS bursts?
[00:05:21] Samir: Quick back-of-envelope: steady 50 QPS with your medium token mix likely needs 1 A100-ish GPU on optimized runtime with batch size ~8 and KV caching. For sustained 220 QPS bursts, to keep p95 under 350–500ms for short replies you'd need roughly 3–4 A100-equivalents with aggressive batching; but because bursts are short you can handle them with a burst pool and autoscale. Exact numbers depend on model choice and quantization. We'll provide a sizing table after we get exact token distributions and model variant preferences.
[00:05:50] Alex: We're planning to run open LLM family models and a tuned LLM for some flows. How much does quantization change sizing?
[00:05:57] Samir: 4-bit quantization can reduce memory and increase throughput but may have a small quality delta. In practice, quantization plus kernel optimizations can give 1.6–2.3x throughput improvement. We'll include model/quant suggestions in the deliverable.

[00:06:10] Priya: On timelines — we'd like a 6-week POC: week 0 data collection and template, week 1 onboarding and infra, week 2 dry-run, week 3 official benchmark, week 4 analysis, week 5 follow-ups and recommended production footprint. Is that feasible?
[00:06:24] Maya: That's reasonable. For many enterprise customers we compress or expand based on readiness. Proposed milestones: data drop by 3/1, harness ready by 3/5, dry-run 3/8, main benchmark 3/15, deliver final report 3/22.
[00:06:36] Nora: That aligns with our internal Q2 plan. We do have a procurement checkpoint at the end of the POC too.

[00:06:43] Alex: A few clarifying things — what do you need for quality/regression checks? We can give a labeled set of 200 prompts and expected outputs approx.
[00:06:51] Samir: That's perfect. We'll run automatic diffing on a small eval suite and also manual scoring for a subset. We'll surface BLEU-like metrics, but more importantly a small panel metric and false-positive rates for hallucination-sensitive flows.

[00:07:05] Priya: There may be regulatory constraints for certain customer cohorts — can we limit data in the POC to non-PII records?
[00:07:11] Maya: Definitely. We recommend scrubbing PII from logs and we'll provide a scrub checklist.

[00:07:16] Jordan: One gotcha — our current API has a 60s upstream timeout. That will impact how you shape long-tail requests in the replay.
[00:07:23] Samir: We'll honor upstream timeouts; in the replay harness we can simulate the same client-side timeouts so benchmarks reflect real behaviour.

[00:07:30] Alex: On metrics reporting, do you produce a per-request breakdown with token-level cost and latency?
[00:07:35] Samir: Yes — our report will include per-request breakdown, aggregated quantiles, and a cost model that extrapolates monthly cost given your projected QPS and token mix. We'll also share a sensitivity table: how p95 changes with batch size and concurrency.

[00:07:50] Nora: For the p95 target for chat we said 350ms — are we measuring inference-only or end-to-end? We need both.
[00:07:56] Samir: We'll report both: inference-only (model runtime) and end-to-end (including network, pre/post processing). We'll also flag cache hit vs miss latency.

[00:08:06] Priya: Regarding compliance docs — we'll need SOC2, data flow, and also any pen test summaries for the hosted infra.
[00:08:12] Maya: We'll share the compliance packet and a summary of our pen test dates.

[00:08:16] Alex: Another question — if we do the replay in our VPC, do you require VPN or will an agent fetch logs from our S3?
[00:08:22] Samir: We support both. The agent model runs inside your VPC and talks to Redwood control plane over an outbound-only channel; for S3 we can pull scrubbed logs but agent is preferred for closed-data requirements.

[00:08:32] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[00:08:34] Maya: Alright let's summarize next steps. Redwood will: send traffic template, provide replay harness, prepare sizing table drafts, and share compliance docs. Pyralis will: scrub and upload 7 days of logs, provide small eval set and confirm that VPC replay is acceptable.
[00:08:50] Alex: We'll aim to drop data by March 1st and confirm VPC run.
[00:08:55] Nora: We'll review the success criteria with product and sign off on the p95/p99 thresholds.
[00:08:59] Priya: Procurement will also need the SOW draft — can you share a sample SOW?
[00:09:03] Maya: Yes, we'll include a sample SOW and POC SLO clause.

[00:09:08] Samir: Quick note on benchmarking details — we'll run three token mixes, three concurrency shapes (steady, ramp, pulse), and capture cold start metrics by simulating idle periods before burst. We'll also produce a short runbook to reproduce the experiments.
[00:09:23] Jordan: Sounds good. For the big bursts, do you recommend pre-warming KV caches?
[00:09:27] Samir: Pre-warm helps, but the workload is heterogeneous so KV pre-warm gives limited benefit unless you can predict keys. We'll measure prefix cache hit rates in the dry-run to quantify the benefit.

[00:09:38] Maya: Any final questions?
[00:09:41] Priya: No, just want to ensure timelines are firm — we'll hold internal checkpoints first week of March.
[00:09:46] Maya: Great. I'll follow up with an email that contains: traffic template link (https://redwood.app/poctemplate), replay harness repo link, checklist for scrubbed logs, and proposed benchmark calendar.
[00:09:58] Alex: Thanks, talk soon.
[00:10:00] Meeting end (note: actual call continued with sidebars, but recording clipped).

Notes on transcription quality: occasional speaker attribution issues and a few misheard technical terms (e.g., K-V cache transcribed as K-V cash), overall medium quality.
